cards.title: 2.1 Magnets, Magnetic Fields, and Electromagnetism
body: 2.1 Magnets, Magnetic Fields, and Electromagnetism

**Magnetism** is a class of physical phenomena mediated by magnetic fields, originating from the motion of electric charges—specifically the spin and orbital motion of electrons—resulting in attractive or repulsive forces between objects.

At the subatomic level, every electron behaves as a microscopic magnetic dipole due to its intrinsic spin and its orbital revolution around the nucleus. In most materials, the magnetic orientations of these electrons point in random directions, canceling each other out. However, in **ferromagnetic** materials like iron, cobalt, and nickel, quantum-mechanical effects cause the magnetic dipoles of adjacent atoms to align parallel to one another. cards.title: Magnetism
body: In 1820, Hans Christian Oersted discovered a direct connection between electricity and magnetism. He observed that an electric current flowing through a wire deflected a nearby compass needle. This demonstrated that moving charges generate their own magnetic fields. For a long, straight, current-carrying wire, the magnetic field lines form concentric circles around the conductor. The direction of these lines is determined by the **Right-Hand Grip Rule**: if you grasp the wire with your right hand so that your thumb points in the direction of the conventional current ($$I$$), your curled fingers point in the direction of the magnetic field vector ($$\mathbf{B}$$). The magnitude of this field at a perpendicular distance $$r$$ from the wire is governed by:
$$B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$$
where $$\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7} \text{ T}\cdot\text{m/A}$$ is the permeability of free space.

cards.title: 2.2 Magnetic Force on Charges and Conductors
body: 2.2 Magnetic Force on Charges and Conductors

The **Lorentz Force** (specifically its magnetic component) is the force exerted on a charged particle moving through a magnetic field, mathematically perpendicular to both the particle's velocity vector and the magnetic field vector.

When a point charge $$q$$ moves with a velocity vector $$\mathbf{v}$$ through an external magnetic field $$\mathbf{B}$$, it experiences a magnetic force $$\mathbf{F}_M$$. The magnitude of this force is given by:
$$F_M = |q| v B \sin \theta$$

where $$\theta$$ is the angle between the velocity vector $$\mathbf{v}$$ and the magnetic field vector $$\mathbf{B}$$. If the charge moves parallel to the field lines ($$\theta = 0^\circ$$ or $$180^\circ$$), the magnetic force is zero. cards.title: Study Notes worked
cards.problem: What is the primary subatomic origin of magnetism in most magnetic materials?

steps.text: **Step 1: Understand the subatomic origin of magnetism**

At the subatomic level, magnetic fields are produced by moving electric charges. In atoms, individual electrons possess an intrinsic property called spin and orbit the nucleus. Both of these motions act as tiny current loops, creating atomic magnetic dipoles.
The nuclear strong force, electrostatic repulsion, and lattice vibrations do not generate magnetic dipoles.
Therefore, the primary origin is the **orbital motion and intrinsic spin of electrons**.

cards.title: Study Notes worked
cards.problem: Which of the following statements about Lenz's Law is true?

steps.text: **Step 1: Define the core physical principle of Lenz's Law**
Lenz's Law states that the induced current's magnetic field must oppose the change in magnetic flux that produced it.

If the induced field reinforced the change in flux, it would create an runaway feedback loop where flux and current increase infinitely without any energy input. This would violate the first law of thermodynamics.
Therefore, Lenz's Law is **a direct consequence of the Conservation of Energy**.

body: material into a permanent or temporary magnet. In contrast, **paramagnetic** materials (like aluminum) show only weak domain alignment in external fields, while **diamagnetic** materials (like bismuth) weakly oppose external fields.

A magnet always possesses two distinct poles: a north-seeking pole (N) and a south-seeking pole (S). If you cut a bar magnet in half, you do not isolate the poles; instead, two new complete dipoles are created, as magnetic monopoles do not exist in nature. The space surrounding a magnet is occupied by a vector quantity called the **Magnetic Field** ($$\mathbf{B}$$), also termed *Magnetic Flux Density*. By convention, magnetic field lines emerge from the north pole, curve through space, and enter the south pole, forming continuous closed loops that never intersect.

cards.title: Magnetism
body: By winding a long wire into a tight coil of $$N$$ turns, we construct a **solenoid**. When an electric current passes through the solenoid, the individual magnetic fields of each loop add together, producing a strong, highly uniform magnetic field inside the coil that resembles the field of a bar magnet. The magnetic field strength inside a long solenoid is calculated by:
$$B = \mu_0 n I = \mu_0 \left(\frac{N}{L}\right) I$$

where $$n$$ is the number of turns per unit length ($$N/L$$). Placing a soft iron core inside the solenoid concentrates the magnetic field lines, greatly increasing the magnetic flux density. This setup is the foundation of **electromagnets**, which are essential for cranes, magnetic relays, electric bells, and speakers.

cards.title: Study Notes worked
cards.problem: Why are the soft iron cores of transformers laminated with thin insulating sheets?

steps.text: **Step 1: Understand the origin of eddy currents**
A changing magnetic flux in the solid iron core of a transformer induces circulating currents within the core material itself.

By cutting the solid core into thin laminations separated by insulation, the path for these circulating currents is disrupted and narrowed. This dramatically increases electrical resistance to these circulating loops, minimizing eddy currents and their associated $$I^2 R$$ heating losses.
Therefore, laminating the core is done **to reduce power loss due to circulating eddy currents**.

cards.title: Magnetism
body: Our planet itself is a giant magnet. The Earth's magnetic field, or geomagnetism, is generated by convective currents of molten iron and nickel in its outer core. Interestingly, the Earth's geographic North Pole corresponds to its magnetic south pole, which is why the north pole of a compass needle points toward geographic north. This magnetic field acts as a protective shield (the magnetosphere), redirecting harmful solar wind particles away from our atmosphere.

cards.title: Magnetism
body: Because the magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity vector, the work done by the magnetic field on the moving charge is exactly zero ($$W = \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{d} = 0$$). Consequently, a magnetic field can change the direction of a charged particle's motion but cannot alter its kinetic energy or speed. When a charged particle enters a uniform magnetic field perpendicularly ($$\theta = 90^\circ$$), the magnetic force acts as a constant centripetal force. This forces the particle to travel in a perfect circle of radius $$r$$:
$$F_C = F_M \implies \frac{m v^2}{r} = q v B \implies r = \frac{m v}{q B}$$
This principle of mass-to-charge ratio separation is used in mass spectrometers and particle accelerators.

cards.title: Study Notes worked
cards.problem: Which of the following modifications will NOT increase the magnetic field inside a current-carrying solenoid?

steps.text: **Step 1: Write down the formula for the magnetic field inside a solenoid**

Increasing $$I$$ or $$N/L$$ increases the field strength. Inserting a soft iron core increases permeability from $$\mu_0$$ to $$\mu$$, drastically increasing the field. Reversing the current direction only reverses the polarity (direction) of the field but does not change its magnitude.
Therefore, **reversing the direction of the current flow** will not increase the field strength.
